title: The Strange World of Dead Internet Protocols

lines.text: Not of websites, but of entire languages that computers once used to communicate.
Before the web took over, there was Gopher.
Instead of clicking through colorful websites, you navigated the internet through simple text menus.
Want to find a file? There was Archie.
It indexed the file listings of public FTP servers, years before web search engines.
And WAIS went further, searching the text inside the documents themselves.
It let you ask a remote computer about a user, sometimes revealing their login, their status, or a personal message.
IPX, from Novell's NetWare, once powered office networks and multiplayer games.

lines.text: X dot twenty-five carried data across telecommunications networks.
lines.display: X.25 carried data across telecommunications networks.

lines.text: Different machines, different rules, different languages.
But here's the interesting part: not everything old disappeared.
lines.display: But here’s the interesting part: not everything old disappeared.

lines.text: IRC and Usenet's NNTP still survive, and Gopher still answers on a few hundred servers.
lines.display: IRC and Usenet’s NNTP still survive, and Gopher still answers on a few hundred servers.

lines.text: Some communities keep using what the mainstream internet left behind.
Protocols are the hidden languages of the internet.
When they disappear from everyday use, their history doesn't vanish.
